[ANSWER]: Existing approaches that achieve linear‑time Gaussian‑process regression on unstructured data typically rely on inducing‑point constructions, which are closely related to Nyström approximations.  An inducing‑point kernel is defined by a set of pseudo‑inputs and a base kernel, and its computational cost scales with the number of inducing points rather than the number of data points.  While such kernels are attractive for their simplicity, they live in a low‑dimensional reproducing‑kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) whose dimensionality is bounded by the number of inducing points, limiting model expressivity.  In contrast, our binary‑tree kernel builds an RKHS whose dimensionality grows exponentially with the depth of the tree, yet the kernel matrix can be assembled in \(O(n)\) space and inverted (approximately) in \(O(n)\) time.  Thus, we retain linear‑time and linear‑space complexity while providing a far richer functional class than traditional inducing‑point kernels.

Sparse Gaussian‑process regression (SGPR) selects a subset of training inputs and forms a low‑rank approximation of the kernel matrix, typically yielding a rank‑\(m\) matrix that can be inverted in \(O(m^{2}n)\) time.  The resulting predictive mean and covariance have compact closed‑form expressions, but the low rank of the approximation constrains the ability of the model to capture complex dependencies.  Our contribution is a kernel that is intrinsically low‑rank in a different sense: the kernel matrix can be expressed as a sum of sparse rank‑one components whose structure is dictated by the binary‑tree hierarchy.  This representation permits exact (up to a controllable approximation) inversion in linear time, offering the same scalability as SGPR while avoiding the severe expressivity bottleneck of a fixed low rank.

Sparse variational Gaussian processes (SVGP) introduce a variational objective over inducing points and optimize both the inducing locations and kernel hyper‑parameters.  The variational formulation provides a principled bound on the marginal likelihood but still inherits the low‑dimensional RKHS of the underlying inducing‑point kernel.  Moreover, the variational bound complicates hyper‑parameter learning and can lead to biased posterior estimates when the inducing set is too small.  By contrast, the binary‑tree kernel is a bona‑fide kernel—not an approximation to another kernel—and its parameters are learned directly by maximizing the exact marginal likelihood (or its tractable approximation).  This yields calibrated uncertainty estimates comparable to full‑GP models, while retaining \(O((n+m)\log(n+m))\) runtime.

Inducing‑frequency methods construct kernels by projecting data onto a set of random Fourier features or other spectral bases.  These approaches are well‑suited to low‑dimensional data and can achieve sub‑linear complexity when the number of frequencies is small, but their performance degrades sharply as dimensionality grows, and the spectral approximation again limits expressivity.  Our binary‑tree kernel does not rely on spectral approximations; instead, it exploits a hierarchical partition of the input space, which yields a kernel that adapts to data structure without sacrificing the ability to model high‑dimensional interactions.  Consequently, we obtain the same logarithmic time complexity as the best inducing‑frequency methods, but with a kernel that is not constrained by a fixed spectral basis.

Tree‑based kernels have been explored in the literature, often for data that is naturally hierarchical (e.g., phylogenetic trees or decision‑tree ensembles).  Earlier works place points on the leaves of a single tree or a collection of trees and define similarity based on shared ancestry, yet their computational cost remains at least quadratic in the number of data points.  Our contribution is to show that, by arranging the leaves in a balanced binary tree and defining the kernel solely via the depth of the deepest common ancestor, the resulting Gram matrix can be stored in linear space and factorized in \(O(n\log n)\) time.  This makes tree‑based kernels practical for large, unstructured regression problems where previous methods were prohibitive.

Finally, a number of recent techniques accelerate exact GP inference by exploiting structure (e.g., Toeplitz or Kronecker algebra) or by using iterative solvers such as conjugate gradients with preconditioning.  While these methods can reduce the per‑iteration cost, their overall runtime depends on the spectrum of the kernel matrix and may require many iterations to converge, leading to unpredictable performance.  Our binary‑tree kernel sidesteps iterative procedures entirely: the kernel matrix admits an explicit decomposition into sparse rank‑one terms, enabling a deterministic \(O((n+m)\log(n+m))\) algorithm for both training and prediction.  In this sense, our work provides a complementary alternative to structured‑matrix and iterative‑solver approaches, offering guaranteed logarithmic scaling and competitive predictive accuracy.

Our contribution directly addresses this vulnerability by embedding a non‑parametric bootstrap within a recursive constraint‑based framework: low‑order independencies, which are empirically stable, are reused throughout the recursion, while higher‑order tests are protected by increasing the number of bootstrap replicates. [ANSWER]: Computational approaches to conceptual metaphor theory have focused on the automatic discovery and representation of metaphorical mappings. The CorMet system extracts conceptual metaphors by modeling selectional preferences of verbs, while later work builds “conceptual spaces” for source domains through rule‑based extraction of lexical relations and uses these spaces to identify new metaphors. Extensions of this pipeline construct repositories that combine linguistic and conceptual metaphor information. Vector‑based methods have been proposed for locating appropriate source domains during metaphor interpretation, and the MetaNet project explores the use of frames to encode metaphorical domains. More recent efforts rely on FrameNet because of its broad coverage and the availability of reliable automatic parsers, enabling the alignment of frames with conceptual domains.

Metaphor generation research initially employed heuristic and template‑driven techniques, such as template‑based generation of creative tweets. Subsequent studies have investigated the creation of metaphorical mappings by clustering WordNet senses, exploiting selectional preferences, mining syntactic proposition databases, or applying embedding‑based models to capture poetic relationships. While these methods generate candidate mappings, they do not directly produce linguistic expressions that realize the mappings. Deep‑learning approaches have addressed metaphor generation by first identifying literal and metaphorical words via selectional restrictions and then training sequence‑to‑sequence models without conditioning on a specific input expression. Other models use masked language modeling to encourage the production of metaphorical tokens, or they collect literal/metaphor pairs to train seq2seq systems for simile generation and metaphorical paraphrasing. Although these systems can generate figurative language, they typically lack explicit grounding in the underlying conceptual metaphors, resulting in outputs that may be metaphorical but are not systematically linked to the source‑target domain relationships that characterize conceptual metaphor theory.

In this work we introduce two metaphor‑generation models that are explicitly grounded in conceptual metaphor theory. The first model is an unsupervised lexical system that leverages FrameNet‑derived embeddings to learn source‑target domain mappings and applies them at the word level. The second model fine‑tunes a pretrained BART encoder‑decoder with source and target domain information, enabling controlled generation of metaphorical paraphrases. We evaluate both models on two tasks: (1) generating metaphoric expressions from known conceptual mappings using a gold‑standard test set, and (2) producing novel expressions from rare or unseen mappings. Comprehensive automatic metrics and human judgments assess basic metaphoricity as well as the presence of the intended conceptual metaphor. The lexical model achieves competitiveness with earlier neural metaphor generators on metaphoricity while surpassing them on domain evocation, and the controlled BART model attains superior performance on both metrics, demonstrating the benefit of incorporating explicit conceptual mappings into metaphor generation.

[ANSWER]: Meta‑learning for reinforcement learning has been explored through a variety of architectural and algorithmic designs. Early approaches represented the learning process with recurrent neural networks, allowing hidden states to persist across episode boundaries and to encode task information [5, 6, 7]. Extensions incorporated temporal convolution and attention mechanisms into recursive architectures to further enhance the representation of task context [8]. Gradient‑based meta‑learning methods such as MAML [9] learn a policy initialization that can be rapidly adapted with a few gradient steps on new tasks, while later work examined how the original sampling distribution influences the final performance [13]. Structured‑exploration strategies have also been proposed to acquire task‑relevant information efficiently [14, 15, 16], and off‑policy methods like PEARL train an encoder that produces a latent context vector conditioning the meta‑RL agent [14].

Within the meta‑RL paradigm, several studies have investigated experience relabeling as a means of sharing data across tasks. One line of work frames meta‑RL as a model‑identification problem, employing context‑dependent neural networks to parameterize transition dynamics and reward functions; this method applies relabeling only at meta‑test time to improve adaptation to out‑of‑distribution tasks, without any data sharing during meta‑training [17]. Another strand addresses offline meta‑RL, introducing reward relabeling to mitigate the “MDP ambiguity” that arises when learning from fixed datasets; the relabeling strategy is based on random task selection and is tailored to the offline setting [18]. Both approaches differ from techniques that aim to increase sample efficiency during the online meta‑training phase.

In multi‑task reinforcement learning, relabeling has been leveraged to enhance sample efficiency across a set of related tasks. Hindsight Experience Replay (HER) substitutes achieved goals for the original ones, enabling learning from sparse binary rewards, but its applicability is limited to goal‑oriented tasks and does not directly extend to meta‑RL where a batch of tasks is sampled from a fixed distribution [22]. More recent methods construct optimal relabeling distributions using maximum‑entropy RL principles, allowing relabeling for both goal‑driven and arbitrary reward functions and demonstrating improvements in multi‑task settings [23, 24].

Building on these strands of research, this work introduces Hindsight Foresight Relabeling (HFR), a novel relabeling scheme for online meta‑RL that combines hindsight replay of trajectories with foresight‑based utility estimation to form a principled relabeling distribution over tasks. By integrating HFR with off‑policy meta‑RL algorithms such as PEARL, the method enables extensive data sharing during meta‑training, thereby improving sample efficiency and asymptotic performance. The approach differs from prior meta‑RL relabeling techniques by operating in the online setting, using a maximum‑entropy‑derived utility to guide task selection, and being compatible with arbitrary reward structures. Empirical evaluation on a suite of robotic manipulation and locomotion benchmarks demonstrates that HFR outperforms existing relabeling methods from both the meta‑RL and multi‑task RL literature, establishing it as the first effective relabeling strategy designed specifically for the meta‑training phase.

While Neely’s approach provides valuable insights into the structure of optimal policies, it does not address the algorithmic challenges of learning these statistics or of delivering finite‑time performance guarantees.  Building on Neely’s formulation, we derive a tractable approximation to the optimal offline policy using Lagrange duality and renewal theory, and we prove that this approximation is asymptotically optimal.  Moreover, we extend the offline results to the online setting by designing a dual‑ascent algorithm that achieves a $\tilde O(B^{-1/2})$ regret bound, thereby advancing the state of the art from purely offline analysis to provably efficient online learning.

Although these techniques succeed in producing visually plausible results, they all learn a single fixed mapping from source to target, which precludes the ability to express predictive uncertainty and makes the models vulnerable to outliers and distribution shifts at test time. In contrast, our Uncertainty‑aware Generalized Adaptive Cycle Consistency (UGAC) framework retains the adversarial and cycle‑consistency objectives of the unpaired literature but augments them with a probabilistic residual model that captures heavy‑tailed error distributions. By doing so, UGAC not only preserves the high‑quality translations of deterministic baselines but also endows each output pixel with a calibrated uncertainty estimate, addressing a key limitation of existing deterministic translators.

Uncertainty estimation for deep generative models has been explored mainly through Bayesian deep learning and heteroscedastic regression, where per‑pixel variance is often assumed Gaussian [9,10,11,12]. While these approaches provide a measure of aleatoric noise, the Gaussian assumption is fragile in the presence of outliers, which commonly follow heavier‑tailed distributions in real‑world imaging scenarios. Recent works have begun to consider more expressive noise models, yet they remain limited to supervised or paired settings and do not integrate uncertainty into the cycle‑consistency framework. UGAC advances this line of research by modeling per‑pixel residuals with a generalized Gaussian distribution, a family that subsumes Gaussian, Laplace, and heavier‑tailed laws. This choice enables robust learning under noisy or corrupted inputs and yields uncertainty scores that correlate strongly with prediction errors, a property not demonstrated by prior Bayesian or heteroscedastic translation methods.

The need for reliable uncertainty quantification is especially acute in safety‑critical domains such as medical image translation, where missing modalities or acquisition artifacts can jeopardize clinical decisions. This positions UGAC as the first unpaired translation model that simultaneously delivers high‑fidelity synthesis, robust outlier handling, and actionable uncertainty information across both natural and medical imaging tasks.

A range of calibration techniques has been proposed, including temperature scaling, confidence‑penalizing regularizers, and loss modifications that encourage smoother output distributions. These methods aim to reduce the certainty of predictions, thereby mitigating the tendency of dialogue systems to produce repetitive or bland utterances.

Although simple, behavior cloning suffers from distribution shift and error accumulation as the learned policy deviates from the demonstrated trajectories. To mitigate these issues, DAgger introduced a no‑regret framework that iteratively queries an oracle for corrective actions, at the cost of requiring online access to the expert. A prominent instance of this paradigm is Generative Adversarial Imitation Learning (GAIL), which casts imitation as a distribution‑matching problem and employs a generative‑adversarial network to minimize the Jensen–Shannon divergence between the expert and learner state‑action distributions. Building on GAIL, numerous works have explored alternative reinforcement‑learning back‑ends or substituted different statistical divergences to improve imitation performance, yet the majority of these approaches remain on‑policy, requiring fresh environment interactions at each policy update and consequently incurring high sample costs.

To address the sample inefficiency of on‑policy imitation, several off‑policy extensions have been proposed. DAC adapts the GAIL objective to reuse past experiences stored in a replay buffer, thereby reducing the need for on‑policy data collection. Similar replay‑based strategies appear in other works that recycle cached transitions for policy improvement. A common limitation of these methods is that they often ignore the distributional discrepancy introduced when substituting the true on‑policy occupancy with an off‑policy approximation, which can lead to a drift from the intended objective. ValueDICE offers another off‑policy route by reformulating the on‑policy imitation loss using the DICE framework; however, it relies on access to expert actions, rendering it unsuitable for settings where only observations are available. Consequently, off‑policy imitation methods that do not require expert actions remain an open challenge.

Learning from Observations (LfO) tackles the more restrictive scenario in which expert action labels are absent. Model‑free LfO approaches typically extend the adversarial imitation paradigm to state‑only data. GAIfO applies the GAIL framework with a discriminator that receives only states, enabling imitation without action information. IDDM analyzes the theoretical gap between LfD and LfO objectives and shows that maximizing the mutual information between latent actions and observed states can partially bridge this gap, achieving performance comparable to GAIL while still relying on on‑policy data. Other model‑free methods assume a ranking over observation trajectories and construct reward functions accordingly; these techniques also inherit the sample‑inefficiency of on‑policy learning.

Model‑based LfO methods introduce dynamics models to compensate for the missing action signals. Forward‑model approaches learn a transition model and use it to synthesize pseudo‑actions or to plan directly; while effective for finite‑horizon tasks, they may struggle with long‑horizon or infinite‑horizon problems due to the need for time‑dependent policies. Inverse‑model approaches infer the missing actions by training a mapping from consecutive observations to the underlying action, after which standard behavior‑cloning can be applied. This strategy, exemplified by Behavior Cloning from Observations (BCO), inherits the limitations of behavior cloning and additionally requires strong assumptions such as deterministic, injective dynamics to guarantee accurate action recovery. Other recent works consider mismatched dynamics or viewpoints between expert and learner observations, further expanding the scope of LfO research.

To further accelerate learning, the method incorporates a regularization term that promotes mode‑covering distribution matching; under deterministic dynamics this regularizer is implemented via an inverse action model learned from the replay buffer. Although effective, these strategies rely on explicit storage of raw images, which raises concerns about memory consumption, privacy, and biological plausibility.

By replaying these features during incremental updates, the methods avoid keeping raw pixels while still providing a signal for past classes. However, the reliance on ImageNet‑pretrained encoders gives them an advantage that may not transfer to domains where the new data differ substantially from the pretraining distribution. Consequently, feature‑based replay can struggle when the target tasks are far removed from the source domain, limiting its applicability in truly continual‑learning scenarios.

Generative replay approaches address the exemplar and feature storage issues by synthesizing past data with learned generators. Early works employ generative adversarial networks (GANs) that are trained jointly on generated samples from earlier classes and real samples from the current task. This continual training can cause semantic drift, whereby the fidelity of regenerated images degrades over successive increments. Some methods mitigate drift by training a separate GAN for each class and freezing its parameters, while using elastic‑weight‑consolidation to protect important weights. Nonetheless, GAN‑based replay often produces samples that lie outside the support of any learned class, which harms classifier performance, especially on complex datasets such as ImageNet. Conditional GANs alleviate this problem to some extent, but their accuracy on large‑scale benchmarks remains limited compared with simpler datasets like MNIST.

While these methods avoid the out‑of‑distribution artifacts typical of GANs, the reconstructed images tend to be blurry, reducing their usefulness for downstream classification. [ANSWER]: Domain adaptation addresses the shift between source and target distributions by designing methods that align or transfer knowledge across domains [1]–[6]. Traditional approaches assume access to target data during training, an assumption that often does not hold in practice. To relax this requirement, recent studies have explored more challenging settings such as few‑shot and one‑shot domain adaptation, where only a limited number of target samples are available for model adjustment [7]–[9].

Domain generalization seeks to learn models that perform well on unseen target domains without any target data at training time. The problem was first introduced in [10] and formally defined in [11]. Early work focused on learning domain‑invariant representations by minimizing feature dissimilarities across source domains [11], [12]. This line of research has been extended by numerous methods that impose invariance constraints on learned features [13]–[17]. An alternative direction augments the source data to expose the model to a broader range of simulated domain shifts, thereby improving robustness to unseen domains [18]–[22].

Meta‑learning has also been applied to domain generalization. Several approaches treat domain generalization as a meta‑learning problem, training on a set of source domains and evaluating adaptation on held‑out domains [23]–[26]. Model‑agnostic meta‑learning (MAML) was introduced for this purpose in [27] and later enhanced with global and local regularization techniques [29]. Common experimental protocols partition source domains into meta‑source and meta‑target subsets to mimic the adaptation process during training [24], [25].

Test‑time adaptation methods aim to adjust a pretrained source model to unseen target data at inference time. Some approaches combine supervised and self‑supervised objectives during source training and then fine‑tune the model on target data using only the self‑supervised loss [31]. Others remove the self‑supervised component and rely on entropy minimization for test‑time fine‑tuning [32]. A different strategy learns a domain‑embedding network from unsupervised source data; the embedding is then estimated for a target domain using many unlabeled target samples, enabling adaptation without explicit fine‑tuning [33]. These techniques typically require additional steps such as fine‑tuning or processing batches of target samples. Test‑time augmentation has also been employed to improve robustness during inference [34], providing another avenue for adapting models to test‑time variations.

[ANSWER]: Marginal‑likelihood approximations have long been a cornerstone of Gaussian‑process (GP) modeling. Early work on sparse GP approximations relied on selecting subsets of the training data to reduce the cubic cost of exact inference, a strategy formalized in the subset‑of‑data (SoD) and subset‑of‑regressors frameworks. The introduction of pseudo‑inputs (or inducing points) provided a more flexible alternative, allowing the inducing locations to be placed anywhere in the input space and leading to variational formulations that yield an evidence lower bound (ELBO) on the marginal likelihood. Stochastic approximations to the ELBO were subsequently proposed, enabling mini‑batch training and scaling to larger datasets. These stochastic ELBO methods can be viewed as Bayesian counterparts to earlier deterministic sparse approximations, preserving the probabilistic treatment while improving scalability.

Active‑set methods, which fix the inducing variables to be a subset of the training inputs, were investigated empirically and shown to produce stable approximations even when the active set comprised only a small fraction of the data. However, random selection of active points was observed to induce non‑smooth fluctuations in the objective, complicating convergence under exact gradient ascent. This instability motivated the development of pseudo‑input approaches, where the inducing variables are optimized continuously rather than chosen discretely, resulting in smoother optimization dynamics. Recent stochastic optimization techniques have revisited active‑set ideas, proposing to average over active‑set configurations rather than optimize a single deterministic subset, thereby mitigating the fluctuations associated with random selection.

The relationship between cross‑validation (CV) and GP marginal‑likelihood estimation has been explored as an alternative avenue for model selection. Initial studies highlighted CV as a practical tool for assessing predictive performance, while later theoretical work established an equivalence between exhaustive CV and the log‑marginal likelihood, offering a novel perspective on Bayesian model evidence. Building on this equivalence, recent research has integrated CV‑based objectives into GP training pipelines. In the context of GP latent‑variable models, back‑constraints have been introduced to regularize the latent space when using inducing points, employing doubly stochastic variational inference to handle the resulting intractabilities. Parallel advances in supervised GP settings have leveraged amortization networks to drastically reduce the number of required inducing points, further enhancing scalability.

In this work we introduce a stochastic active‑set (SAS) framework that unifies these strands of prior research. By exploiting the established link between exhaustive cross‑validation and the log‑marginal likelihood, we derive a stochastic estimator of the marginal likelihood that can be evaluated efficiently using randomly sampled active sets. Unlike traditional active‑set methods, SAS does not seek a single optimal subset; instead, it averages over many subsets, eliminating the non‑smooth fluctuations observed with random selection and obviating the need for costly combinatorial optimization. This stochastic estimation also sidesteps the optimization challenges associated with pseudo‑inputs, while retaining the computational benefits of fixed active points. Moreover, SAS integrates naturally with back‑constraint ideas, providing a principled way to encourage structure in the latent space without additional variational parameters. Empirically, the SAS‑GP decoder attains superior latent representations, scales to substantially larger datasets, and outperforms both variational autoencoders and competing GP‑based decoders in terms of robustness, computational efficiency, and representation quality.

[ANSWER]: Post‑processing of pretrained classifiers is a widely studied avenue for attaining fairness, alongside approaches that jointly train a fair model or combine multiple models.  Early work in the “model‑retraining’’ family (e.g., [2]–[5]) imposes a dual objective: remain close to the original black‑box while satisfying a fairness constraint.  These methods typically rely on constrained optimisation or adversarial training, which limits their flexibility to accommodate many fairness notions and often requires access to the original training data.  In contrast, our technique operates purely as a wrapper around a fixed predictor, requiring no retraining or data access, and therefore directly addresses desideratum (a) – the ability to handle a broad spectrum of fairness metrics – while also satisfying (b) through provable proximity guarantees between the original and modified posteriors.

A second line of research modifies the classifier’s outputs at inference time, either by adjusting decision thresholds ([6]–[10]) or by learning a mapping from predictions to fair outcomes ([5], [6]).  These approaches achieve pointwise fairness guarantees but rarely provide systematic bounds on how far the transformed distribution deviates from the original, nor do they offer composability when multiple fairness corrections are applied sequentially.  Our contribution fills this gap: by learning an α‑tree wrapper based on the α‑loss, we obtain explicit KL‑divergence bounds (addressing (b) and (c)), a clean composability property (addressing (e)), and an interpretable tree‑shaped representation (addressing (d)).  Moreover, the α‑loss framework guarantees that any “twist’’ in the prediction—including unfair bias—can be corrected, a capability absent from prior post‑processing methods.

The third category exploits ensembles of classifiers to achieve fairness, either by aggregating models trained under different constraints ([11]) or by selecting subsets that satisfy fairness criteria ([12]).  While ensembles can improve robustness, they inherit the limitations of their constituent models and often depend on convex optimisation procedures whose computational cost is not clearly characterised.  Our approach differs fundamentally: rather than combining multiple black‑boxes, we construct a single, lightweight α‑tree that directly modifies the output of any black‑box.  This yields a clear algorithmic cost—two boosting procedures with provable convergence—addressing the “algorithmic price‑tag’’ concern (c) and providing strong generalisation guarantees (f) via Rademacher‑complexity analysis.

Finally, recent studies have explored improper loss functions for fair probability estimation ([4], [11]), yet none have leveraged the specific properties of the α‑loss to obtain universal correction of unfairness.  By building on the improper‑loss analysis of Nock (2021), we are the first to demonstrate how the α‑loss can be harnessed in a post‑processing wrapper that simultaneously satisfies the full suite of desiderata (a)–(f).  Our empirical evaluation on conditional value‑at‑risk, equality of opportunity, and statistical parity further confirms that the proposed α‑tree boosters outperform existing baselines across diverse datasets.

[ANSWER]: A large body of work has addressed convex‑concave saddle‑point problems using first‑order methods such as Gradient Descent‑Ascent, ExtraGradient, Optimistic Gradient Descent‑Ascent, Hamiltonian Gradient Descent and Consensus Optimization. These algorithms are known to converge linearly when the objective is strongly convex in the primal variable and strongly concave in the dual variable, but their iteration complexity depends on condition numbers in a sub‑optimal way. By contrast, the algorithm introduced in this paper—Proximal Best Response—achieves linear convergence with a gradient‑complexity bound that scales as \(\tilde O\!\Bigl(\sqrt{\frac{L_x}{m_x}+\frac{L\cdot L_{xy}}{m_xm_y}+\frac{L_y}{m_y}}\log\frac1\epsilon\Bigr)\). This dependence is strictly tighter than that of the classic methods whenever the cross‑smoothness constant \(L_{xy}\) is smaller than the largest smoothness constant \(L\), which is precisely the regime where many machine‑learning applications exhibit weak interaction between the two players.

Lower‑bound constructions for saddle‑point problems have been established for both convex‑concave and strongly convex‑strongly concave settings. In particular, Zhang et al. (2019) and Ibrahim et al. (2019) proved a gradient‑complexity lower bound of \(\Omega\!\Bigl(\sqrt{\frac{L_x}{m_x}+\frac{L_{xy}^2}{m_xm_y}+\frac{L_y}{m_y}}\log\frac1\epsilon\Bigr)\) that applies to any first‑order method. The bound derived in this work matches that lower bound up to a sub‑polynomial factor, and it does so for the full class of smooth, strongly convex‑strongly concave functions rather than for restricted algorithmic families. Consequently, our result establishes (near) optimality of the proposed method in the sense of first‑order oracle complexity.

Recent algorithmic advances have tightened the dependence on condition numbers for the strongly convex‑strongly concave case. Lin et al. (2020) obtained an upper bound of \(\tilde O\!\bigl(\sqrt{L^2/(m_xm_y)}\,\log^3(1/\epsilon)\bigr)\), which improves over earlier results but still suffers from a cubic logarithmic factor and from a condition‑number term that becomes loose when the interaction between the variables is weak (i.e., when \(L_{xy}\ll L\)). Moreover, the bound of Lin et al. does not guarantee a linear convergence rate. The Proximal Best Response algorithm presented here eliminates both drawbacks: it enjoys a linear rate and a condition‑number dependence that adapts to the magnitude of \(L_{xy}\), thereby strictly improving the guarantees of Lin et al. in all regimes of interest.

A complementary line of research has focused on the bilinear saddle‑point structure, where the coupling term is of the form \(x^\top By\). Our analysis treats the general smooth interaction directly, and the resulting complexity bound reduces to the bilinear case when \(L_{xy}=L\), thus encompassing and improving upon the existing bilinear results without requiring additional variance‑reduction machinery.

[ANSWER]: Most research on interpretability in deep natural‑language processing has been organized around two complementary questions: (i) which linguistic or non‑linguistic knowledge is encoded in contextualized representations (often termed concept analysis), and (ii) how that information influences the model’s decision‑making process (attribution analysis). The concept‑analysis line of work typically adopts a post‑hoc decomposability stance, examining trained models to reveal linguistic phenomena that emerge during training on various NLP tasks. In contrast, attribution studies focus on attributing predictions to particular model components or input features. Both strands have produced extensive literature that explores the internal workings of neural language models.

A large body of work employs visualization techniques to expose the structure of learned representations, including analyses of hidden states, attention heads, and compositionality patterns. A widely adopted methodology is the probing framework, in which auxiliary classifiers are trained on frozen representations to predict linguistic properties such as morphology, syntax, or semantics. Probing has been applied to a broad range of granularity levels—from character‑ and word‑level tasks to sub‑sentence phenomena—providing quantitative evidence of the information retained at different network depths. Complementary to probing, several studies have identified individual neurons or subnetworks that are highly predictive of specific linguistic attributes, or that are salient for model behavior irrespective of any predefined property.

Investigations that go beyond probing to discover latent concepts directly in the representation space have also emerged. Some authors have examined the organization of hidden states in pre‑trained models, revealing clusters that correspond to interpretable linguistic categories. Other approaches induce latent concepts by training binary classifiers on a downstream task, then interpreting the resulting decision boundaries as concept representations. These studies demonstrate that models can encode both linguistically motivated and novel, task‑specific concepts, although they often rely on supervised signals to define the concepts of interest.

Critiques of the probing paradigm have highlighted methodological concerns such as the dependence on probe complexity, the influence of random seeds, and the risk of conflating representational capacity with learnability. These limitations have motivated the development of alternative, probe‑free analyses that aim to characterize the intrinsic geometry of the representation space without auxiliary training. Nonetheless, probing and unsupervised concept discovery are generally viewed as complementary tools for elucidating the knowledge encoded in neural language models.

In this paper we introduce a novel, unsupervised framework for analyzing encoded concepts in contextualized word representations. By clustering layer‑wise activations with hierarchical agglomerative methods and aligning the resulting clusters to a broad suite of human‑defined linguistic categories—including affixation, casing, morphological, syntactic, semantic, WordNet, and psycholinguistic concepts—we obtain quantitative and qualitative measurements of how knowledge is structured across model depths. Our analysis, applied to seven transformer‑based language models, reveals that lower layers predominantly capture shallow lexical phenomena, while middle and higher layers encode core linguistic properties such as morphology, syntax, and semantics. Moreover, roughly half of the discovered clusters correspond to existing human‑defined concepts, whereas the remainder exhibit multi‑faceted patterns that cannot be readily explained by the predefined taxonomy, indicating the emergence of novel internal concepts. By avoiding the probe‑training step, our approach sidesteps the methodological pitfalls associated with probing while remaining compatible with probe‑based findings, thereby providing a scalable and complementary perspective on representation interpretability.

One line of work uses the largest eigenvalue of the Hessian, while a follow‑up employs the trace of the Hessian to gauge each layer’s susceptibility to perturbations. The underlying intuition is that strong curvature near a minimum indicates that small weight changes will significantly affect the loss, guiding the allocation of higher precision to sensitive layers.

A Bayesian perspective on mixed‑precision quantization has been explored by methods that infer per‑tensor bit widths from the uncertainty of weights in a variational posterior. Although this approach provides a principled probabilistic treatment, it does not enforce explicit control over the resulting bit widths, which can lead to configurations that are suboptimal for hardware implementation.

Mixed‑precision search has also been framed as a neural architecture search problem. In one formulation, each layer maintains separate weight copies for every candidate bit width, and a stochastic variant of DARTS is employed to learn the optimal bit‑width assignment jointly with the network parameters. This strategy integrates bit‑width selection into the architecture optimization loop.

Reinforcement‑learning based methods treat bit‑width assignment as a decision problem. An agent observes layer‑level characteristics and selects a bit width from a discrete action space; after a brief fine‑tuning phase, the validation accuracy serves as a reward. Some designs augment the reward with direct feedback from target hardware, enabling the agent to adapt to device‑specific constraints without relying on proxy metrics.

Independent works have shown that learning the quantization scale together with model parameters improves fixed‑bit‑width networks. By redefining the quantization operation to expose a learnable scale, these methods jointly optimize scale and weights. Residual vector quantization (RVQ) recursively quantizes the residual error left after an initial quantization step, a concept originally applied to compress vectors with K‑means. Extending RVQ to neural networks, weight compression methods store only the centroids of K‑means‑quantized vectors, achieving substantial model size reductions. The gating variables are optimized through variational inference with priors that favor low‑bit solutions, while an efficient approximation makes the objective amenable to standard gradient descent. Methods for learning data augmentation policies, reweighting schemes, and other data‑centric strategies also adopt a nested formulation, optimizing augmentation parameters or sample weights based on validation performance [21–25]. [ANSWER]: The literature on sample‑efficient sequential decision‑making has long emphasized principled information‑acquisition strategies, most notably information‑directed sampling (IDS) and its variants. These works establish the information ratio as a clean objective that balances expected regret against information gain about the optimal action, and they provide elegant theoretical guarantees for algorithms that minimize this ratio. However, all existing formulations measure information solely with respect to the optimal action, implicitly assuming that the designer’s learning target is fixed and optimal. In contrast, our contribution is to extend the IDS framework so that the information ratio quantifies regret and information gain about *any* learning target computed via rate‑distortion theory. By doing so, we preserve the analytical tractability of IDS while enabling designers to specify a spectrum of satisficing targets, thereby directly addressing the gap between efficient information acquisition and flexible target selection.

Parallel strands of research have applied rate‑distortion theory to sequential decision problems, showing that the minimal number of bits required to identify a target can be traded off against a tolerable performance shortfall. Prior work operationalizes the Blahut‑Arimoto algorithm to compute such satisficing targets and embeds them within a Thompson‑sampling policy (the BLASTS algorithm). Although BLASTS demonstrates that agents can automatically adjust their learning target over time, it inherits the sub‑optimal exploration behavior of probability‑matching, which limits sample efficiency. Our work builds on this foundation by replacing the Thompson‑sampling component with an IDS‑based action selection rule, yielding the Blahut‑Arimoto Information‑Directed Sampling (BLAIDS) algorithm. BLAIDS retains the single‑parameter control over the target‑performance trade‑off while achieving strictly better regret‑information trade‑offs than BLASTS, thereby unifying optimal target computation with optimal information acquisition.

A third line of research focuses on the Blahut‑Arimoto algorithm itself, which is celebrated in information theory for solving rate‑distortion problems via alternating optimization. Numerous studies have refined its convergence properties and computational speed, yet these advances have not been leveraged in the context of sequential decision‑making. Our paper adopts the classical Blahut‑Arimoto routine as a black‑box sub‑procedure for generating learning targets, but we deliberately keep the algorithmic core unchanged to isolate the effect of the novel IDS‑based exploration scheme. By doing so, we provide a clear baseline that demonstrates the performance gains attributable solely to the new information‑ratio formulation, while also highlighting that future work could further accelerate BLAIDS by incorporating recent Blahut‑Arimoto enhancements.

Finally, while earlier efforts have either (i) focused exclusively on optimal‑action information (IDS) or (ii) on satisficing‑target computation without optimal exploration (BLASTS), no prior work has presented a unified algorithm that simultaneously optimizes both dimensions. Our contribution fills this exact niche: we introduce a principled, hyperparameter‑controlled method for jointly designing learning targets via rate‑distortion theory and acquiring information about them through a generalized information‑directed sampling rule. Empirically, we show that BLAIDS outperforms both vanilla IDS (which lacks target flexibility) and BLASTS (which lacks optimal exploration), establishing a new state‑of‑the‑art for sample‑efficient, target‑aware sequential decision‑making.

[ANSWER]: Analyzing the expressive power of coupling‑based normalizing flows has been an active research topic. A foundational result shows that any coupling‑based flow capable of approximating an arbitrary invertible function can learn any probability density in the weak sense [1]. This universality has been established for affine coupling flows [2, 3, 4], Flow++ [5], neural autoregressive flows [6] and SOS polynomial flows [7]. Similar universality statements for affine coupling flows in Wasserstein distance have also been proved [8]. These works, however, rely on couplings becoming increasingly ill‑conditioned as the approximation error diminishes, a phenomenon that is rarely observed in practice where learned functions tend to remain smooth. Moreover, the analyses are restricted to finite‑dimensional subspaces of the data domain and employ convergence criteria (weak convergence or Wasserstein distance) that do not guarantee convergence under the Kullback‑Leibler (KL) divergence, the loss actually optimized in maximum‑likelihood training. Indeed, an arbitrarily small distance in those metrics can correspond to an infinite KL divergence.

The relationship between conditioning of the coupling layers and the class of distributions that can be modeled has been examined in several studies. It has been shown that well‑conditioned affine couplings are sufficient to approximate log‑concave distributions that have been padded with additional dimensions, again with guarantees expressed in Wasserstein distance [9]. In contrast, Lipschitz‑constrained flows cannot capture arbitrary tail behaviours; this limitation can be mitigated by suitably adapting the latent distribution [10].

Beyond affine couplings, other families of normalizing flows have been investigated with respect to their convergence properties. SOS polynomial flows have been proven to converge in total variation to arbitrary probability densities [11], a mode of convergence that likewise does not imply KL convergence. Zero‑padded affine coupling flows have been shown to converge weakly [12], and Neural Ordinary Differential Equation (Neural ODE) based flows enjoy weak convergence guarantees as well [13, 14].

Meanwhile, [6] focuses on extracting result values, but only in the context of pre-defined TDM triples, making it similar in limitation to [1]. Consequently, these methods are not adaptable to the dynamic nature of emerging benchmarks, where new tasks, datasets, and metrics are frequently introduced.
In a parallel research thread, scientific leaderboards have been treated as a form of scientific knowledge graphs composed of Task, Dataset, and Metric entities. Information extraction in this context has been widely studied, as seen in works such as [5, 7, 8, 9, 10]. These studies typically focus on linking scientific content to structured entities but often assume that the schema or triples are known in advance.
In contrast to prior work, our approach addresses several critical limitations. We construct our dataset manually from publications to ensure comprehensive TDMR annotations, rather than relying on incomplete or unstandardized third-party sources. We normalize TDMR tuples for accurate leaderboard construction and propose novel experimental settings that reflect realistic, dynamic scenarios, including cold-start conditions without any pre-defined TDM taxonomy. By simultaneously constructing a scientific knowledge graph and linking publications to it in an open-domain setting, our method is inherently adaptable to the evolving research landscape.

Early work employed GMs to approximate volumetric data ([5]), while later studies introduced probabilistic models of point clouds based on GMs ([6], [7]). These attributes can be treated as feature vectors attached to points, making prior work on point‑cloud processing relevant; an extensive survey of such methods is given in [11].  

Point convolutional networks have been proposed by several authors ([12]–[17]). Notably, Atzmon et al. construct a mixture by assigning a Gaussian with uniform variance to each point, yielding a coarse fitting of the point cloud. After analytical convolution, the result is sampled at the original point locations, which can lead to loss of information away from those points and effectively implements a weighting function for neighboring points.  

Radial Basis Function Networks also learn Gaussian mixtures to detect patterns in input data ([18]). While these networks share the use of radial basis functions, their primary goal is pattern detection on a set of data points, akin to multilayer perceptrons, rather than performing convolutional operations on another set of radial basis functions.

[ANSWER]: A large body of work replaces the simple average of individual losses in empirical risk minimization with alternative aggregation operators.  Min‑max formulations that minimize the largest loss have been employed to enforce fairness across sub‑populations, to obtain robustness against adversarial perturbations, and to improve generalization to unseen domains.  Recent studies have interpreted such operators as smooth approximations to the max, often using LogSumExp or related super‑quantile constructions, and have shown that they can be solved efficiently when the smoothing parameter is moderate.  Our tilted empirical risk minimization (TERM) framework subsumes these approaches: by introducing a single tunable tilt parameter we obtain a continuously differentiable objective that interpolates between the average loss, various super‑quantiles, and the exact max‑loss.  Unlike prior smooth‑max methods, TERM remains analytically tractable for a wide range of tilt values, enabling fast first‑order optimization while preserving the ability to target any desired loss quantile.  Consequently, TERM provides a unified, computationally efficient alternative to the disparate min‑max and super‑quantile techniques that have previously been treated as separate solutions.

Another line of research modifies the loss function itself in order to mitigate outliers, address class imbalance, or promote fairness.  Robust regression methods replace the squared loss with Huber, Tukey, or general M‑estimators; curriculum‑learning and hard‑example mining strategies amplify large losses; and fairness‑oriented designs impose constraints or alter the loss shape to equalize subgroup performance.  Some recent proposals introduce exponentially tilted losses, but they are typically limited to specific base losses (e.g., squared loss) and correspond to a single tilt setting.  In contrast, TERM can be interpreted as an exponential reshaping of any base loss, with the tilt parameter governing a smooth transition from down‑weighting extreme losses (thereby suppressing outliers) to up‑weighting them (thereby focusing on hard examples).  This single, principled formulation simultaneously captures the effect of many bespoke loss designs and, as we demonstrate, can be extended hierarchically to achieve multi‑objective trade‑offs that were previously unattainable with standard loss modifications.

A third family of approaches influences the learning objective indirectly by re‑weighting individual samples.  Common strategies include class‑wise subsampling, loss‑based importance weighting in stochastic optimization, regularization‑induced weighting, loss clipping, and modeling annotator reliability.  These methods often require problem‑specific heuristics, additional hyper‑parameters, or ad‑hoc clipping thresholds, and their theoretical properties are typically limited to particular settings.  TERM implicitly implements a dynamic, loss‑dependent re‑weighting: the gradient of the tilted objective assigns weights to samples that are an exponential function of their current loss values, and Lemma X shows that this weighting is a convexified version of classic loss clipping.  Because the re‑weighting emerges naturally from a smooth, globally defined objective, TERM inherits convergence guarantees for any smooth loss and any tilt value, and it avoids the need for external weighting schemes.  Our experiments confirm that TERM matches or exceeds the performance of state‑of‑the‑art re‑weighting methods across a range of tasks, thereby establishing TERM as a general, theoretically grounded alternative to existing sample‑weighting techniques.

These approaches have demonstrated that raw softmax scores often over‑confidently misrepresent true correctness, motivating a broad literature on post‑hoc and training‑time calibration strategies.

Within neural machine translation (NMT), research on calibration is considerably sparser. Initial analyses revealed that NMT models appear well‑calibrated during training but become severely miscalibrated at inference time, especially when predicting sentence termination tokens (Kumar et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2020). Subsequent investigations confirmed that the softmax probabilities assigned to generated tokens do not reliably reflect translation quality (Müller et al., 2019). Despite these findings, systematic methods for improving calibration in NMT remain limited, and most existing work focuses on diagnosing the problem rather than providing practical remedies.

Monte Carlo dropout has been proposed as a way to capture model uncertainty in NMT by performing multiple stochastic forward passes and aggregating the resulting predictions (Gal & Ghahramani, 2016; DeVries & Taylor, 2018). While this technique can yield richer uncertainty estimates, it incurs substantial computational overhead and is difficult to scale to large‑scale Transformer architectures. Alternative Bayesian approaches, such as variational inference over the model parameters, have faced similar efficiency challenges, limiting their adoption in production translation systems.

Quality estimation (QE) for machine translation seeks to predict translation quality without reference texts. Supervised QE models have achieved strong performance by training on large corpora of human‑annotated quality scores (Kim et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2021). Early large‑scale collections such as ImageNet demonstrated that growing data volume can simultaneously introduce subtle correlations, for example background cues that leak object class information. Subsequent crowd‑sourced resources amplified this issue, as annotators inject uncontrolled socio‑economic signals that become entangled with the target labels. In visual question answering, analyses revealed that questions alone often suffice to predict correct answers, prompting re‑annotation efforts and revised train‑test splits to mitigate language‑only shortcuts. Similar observations were made for audio‑visual scene‑aware dialog, where the textual query can dominate over visual and acoustic streams, and for natural language inference datasets where lexical heuristics correlate with labels. Story‑completion corpora have also been shown to admit length‑based predictors that bypass narrative understanding. More recently, the SocialIQ benchmark, intended for social‑situational reasoning, was found to be solvable with text alone because sentiment cues strongly align with the correct statements, highlighting the persistence of modality‑specific biases across diverse tasks.

A variety of techniques have been proposed to reduce or compensate for such dataset biases. Approaches that target known biased attributes—such as gender in vision—often mask or remove the corresponding visual regions, or explicitly re‑balance training distributions using test‑set statistics. In the context of visual question answering, several methods train an auxiliary classifier on the question modality and use its predictions to regularize the main model, either by masking softmax outputs, employing product‑of‑experts formulations, or jointly optimizing a full model together with a question‑only expert. These strategies share the reliance on a subset classifier to expose and attenuate the influence of biased cues. While effective at limiting shortcut learning, they differ from methods that evaluate bias by directly perturbing input modalities after training.

Feature‑importance and interpretability techniques provide complementary insights into model behavior at the level of individual inputs. Local surrogate models such as LIME approximate a linear explanation around a specific instance, whereas DeepLIFT and SHAP compute attribution scores based on back‑propagation or Shapley value approximations, respectively. Extensions that combine DeepLIFT with Shapley theory (Deep SHAP) further refine these estimates. Other work investigates cross‑modal interactions by approximating a multimodal predictor with a set of single‑modality models, thereby quantifying the benefit of modality fusion. These methods focus on fine‑grained feature contributions, whereas the emerging need is for metrics that assess the reliance on an entire modality in a unified and model‑agnostic manner.

In this work we introduce a simple, model‑agnostic metric—the perceptual score—that quantifies how much a multimodal classifier depends on each input modality. By permuting the features of a given modality across test samples after training, the score measures the drop in performance attributable to the disruption of that modality’s information. We apply this metric to a broad collection of visual question answering and visual dialog models across several benchmark datasets, uncovering a consistent trend in which newer, higher‑accuracy models rely increasingly on textual cues while neglecting visual input. The perceptual score also enables a fine‑grained bias analysis by decomposing the overall reliance into contributions from specific data subsets, such as question types. Our experiments demonstrate that the metric can reveal hidden modality‑specific shortcuts, complement existing bias‑reduction strategies, and provide a practical tool for evaluating and improving the perceptiveness of multimodal systems.

[ANSWER]: Few‑shot learning (FSL) methods are typically organized into three families. The first family expands the training set using prior knowledge, often through hand‑crafted data augmentations such as geometric reflections or more sophisticated transformations. The second family restricts the hypothesis space by embedding prior constraints, for example by regularizing model parameters or imposing structural priors. The third family modifies the search strategy in the hypothesis space, for instance by employing early‑stopping criteria that incorporate external knowledge about task difficulty.  

Building on the ideas of FSL, few‑shot domain adaptation (FDA) incorporates limited target‑domain supervision into the adaptation process. Representative approaches include methods that pair source and target examples and apply adversarial alignment, as well as techniques that exploit invariant causal mechanisms across domains in a meta‑distributional setting. Although these FDA strategies reduce the amount of target data required, they generally assume access to a sizable labeled source dataset, which can raise privacy concerns when source data contain sensitive information.  

Hypothesis transfer learning (HTL) addresses a setting in which only a pretrained source‑domain classifier is available, together with a small set of labeled target examples or a larger pool of unlabeled target data. Early work leveraged leave‑one‑out error estimates to tune transfer parameters using limited labeled target samples. Subsequent methods froze the source classifier and learned target‑specific feature extractors from abundant unlabeled target data, or employed image‑translation techniques to map target images into the source style. A two‑stage learning framework has also been proposed for universal HTL scenarios. While HTL reduces dependence on source data, it still requires a non‑trivial amount of target information, such as several labeled examples per class or a modest labeling proportion, distinguishing it from settings that operate with only a single example per class.

These approaches output an ordered list and treat it as if it were unordered, which gives rise to the responsibility problem. Some point‑cloud methods mitigate this issue by imposing domain‑specific assumptions, for example assuming independence of points within a set [7] or exploiting grid‑like structures [8]. To avoid the computational cost of graph‑matching losses, permutation‑invariant losses have been computed in latent space, for instance by comparing graphs adversarially [9].

Another line of work employs recurrent neural network (RNN) decoders to generate the list representation [10‑12]. When a canonical ordering can be derived from domain knowledge, the set prediction problem simplifies to a sequence problem [12]; an example is the generation of graph nodes ordered by a breadth‑first‑search traversal [13].

Iterative energy‑minimisation approaches have also been explored. Mordatch [14] introduced a method that iteratively minimises an energy function within each forward pass and differentiates through the iteration to learn network parameters. This technique has been demonstrated on small 2‑D element sets, showing the feasibility of differentiable optimisation loops for set‑structured outputs. Zhang et al. [15] constructed an auto‑encoder that pools a set into a feature vector and shares encoder information with a permutation‑equivariant decoder, thereby avoiding the responsibility problem; however, the requirement of an encoder at inference time restricts the approach to auto‑encoding rather than open‑set prediction. Greff et al. [16] proposed an auto‑encoder with a set‑structured latent space for images, enabling the discovery of latent object sets under task‑specific assumptions, which is of interest for representation learning.

The idea of using back‑propagation through an optimisation process as a decoder originates from introspective neural networks [17, 18], where the optimisation loops for prediction and weight learning are performed sequentially. Subsequent work on nested optimisation for structured outputs [19, 20] generalises this concept, allowing the outer optimisation to differentiate through the inner optimisation. Related studies also differentiate through optimisation procedures, as in [14] and [16], highlighting the broader applicability of such techniques to set‑valued outputs. In contrast, differentiating through a decoder to learn representations rather than predictions has been investigated in [21].

It is useful to distinguish vector‑to‑set settings from set‑to‑set mappings. Equivariant variants of Deep Sets [22] and self‑attention mechanisms [23] address set‑to‑set transformations, where the output ordering typically mirrors the input and the responsibility problem does not arise. Methods that predict permutation matrices for sets, effectively converting a set to a list, have been studied in [24, 25]. These approaches require an input set, whereas vector‑to‑set models are necessary for tasks such as object detection, where the input is a feature vector derived from an image encoder and must be transformed into an output set.

Subsequent algorithmic work has focused on promoting fair exposure for individual items or for protected groups of items.  Typical objectives include preventing winner‑take‑all dynamics, mitigating popularity bias, and increasing the visibility of smaller producers.  These approaches generally formulate item‑side fairness as a constraint or regularizer on exposure, often aiming for equal (or quality‑weighted) exposure across items.

Research on two‑sided fairness has extended the focus to users as well as items.  One line of work introduces user‑side fairness by applying concave transformations to user utilities, thereby giving higher marginal weight to less‑served users.  Another strand relies on equality constraints to enforce uniform user satisfaction, while a third proposes envy‑free rankings for users together with a guaranteed minimum share of exposure for items.  Although these methods incorporate both sides, they typically lack a mechanism for smoothly trading off user and item utilities, and they often depend on fixed fairness definitions rather than allowing adjustable compromises.

Fairness considerations in reciprocal recommendation settings have received comparatively less attention.  Some studies aim to equalize utility across user groups, but they inherit the same limitations of single‑metric inequality reductions.  Other approaches adopt a welfare‑function perspective but optimize only the utility of the users being recommended, ignoring the impact on the recommending users.  Post‑processing techniques have been proposed to correct inconsistencies between estimated and declared user preferences, yet they assume that bias in the underlying preference estimates has already been resolved.  Separate lines of work address fairness in matching problems such as ridesharing, but these focus on allocation rather than ranking.  

A growing body of literature connects fairness in machine learning with concepts from social choice theory and welfare economics.  Studies have examined parity penalties in classification tasks and highlighted the importance of Pareto‑efficiency as a criterion for fair outcomes.  This perspective has motivated the integration of economic notions such as Lorenz curves and welfare functions into algorithmic fairness, though most prior work has been limited to classification or single‑side settings.

Theoretical analysis shows that the method always yields rankings with non‑dominated generalized Lorenz curves, overcoming the shortcomings of existing constraint‑based and single‑metric approaches. [ANSWER]: Memory‑based approaches address catastrophic forgetting by re‑introducing information from earlier tasks during the training of new ones.  Some methods store raw exemplars from previous datasets and interleave them with data from the current task, thereby preserving performance on earlier categories.  Other techniques retain only a subset of past examples or compress them into a small buffer and use gradient‑based criteria to reduce interference between the old and new objectives.  A related line of work trains generative models—such as GANs or autoencoders—to synthesize samples that approximate past data distributions, offering a memory‑efficient alternative to explicit storage.  Still‑another family saves feature representations of prior instances and learns transformations that map these stored features into the space of the current task, again limiting the amount of retained raw data.

Regularization‑ and architecture‑based strategies aim to limit how much a new task can modify the parameters that are important for previously learned problems.  Weight‑regularization methods add explicit penalties that keep critical weights close to their earlier values, while mask‑based techniques freeze selected subsets of the network during the learning of subsequent tasks.  Some works increase the model’s capacity by allocating additional parameters for each incoming task, often coupled with mechanisms that decide how to partition the expanded network.  Variants of this paradigm search for task‑specific pathways through a shared backbone, freezing the identified routes and restricting further adaptation, or employ specialized components such as hypernetworks, deep artificial neurons, or compositional structures to provide flexible, reusable modules across tasks.

Meta‑learning, the paradigm of “learning to learn,” has been incorporated into sequential and continual learning settings to improve adaptation to new tasks while mitigating forgetting.  Approaches have leveraged meta‑optimization to shape initializations that are amenable to rapid fine‑tuning on successive problems, or to construct instance‑level prototypes that guide weight updates in a way that preserves prior knowledge.  Several recent studies combine meta‑learning objectives with continual‑learning constraints, demonstrating that meta‑trained learners can exhibit reduced interference when presented with a stream of tasks.  However, most of these works focus on shaping the learning dynamics rather than maintaining an explicit, incrementally updated knowledge repository.

Weight‑conditioning mechanisms modify network parameters in a data‑dependent manner, often by using auxiliary signals to adapt layer outputs.  Techniques such as feature‑wise linear modulation normalize convolutional activations through learned scaling and shifting functions, while other methods condition convolutional responses on external inputs like questions in visual‑question‑answering systems.  These conditioning schemes provide a way to steer the network’s computation without permanently altering the underlying weights, yet they have typically been applied as isolated modules rather than as part of a larger framework for continual knowledge accumulation.

In this work we introduce a continual‑learning method that unifies the advantages of the aforementioned streams.  By employing a meta‑learning procedure we construct a shared knowledge base whose parameters are incrementally enriched as new tasks arrive, while a set of trainable masks implements a selective addressing mechanism that queries the most relevant subset of the base for each task.  This design simultaneously mitigates catastrophic forgetting through weight reusability, avoids the need for extensive replay buffers or generative replay, and circumvents the parameter explosion associated with naïve capacity expansion.  Empirical evaluation on standard benchmarks demonstrates state‑of‑the‑art accuracy improvements of more than ten percent on large‑scale splits, with near‑zero forgetting and using roughly half the parameters of competing methods.  An ablation study confirms that the learned masks effectively isolate task‑specific knowledge within the shared repository, validating the proposed synergy between meta‑learning‑driven knowledge accumulation and conditional weight selection.

These methods typically operate in two stages: first learning a goal‑conditioned policy, then integrating that policy with a graph‑search planner. This stage‑wise approach has yielded impressive results on challenging control problems, including real‑world robotic navigation [10, 11]. However, the post‑hoc use of graph search prevents the search procedure from influencing the underlying policy, and the quality of the collected data remains a critical factor for RL performance [15–17].  

Exploration is another central theme in goal‑conditioned RL. The effectiveness of exploration depends heavily on how goals are sampled, a problem addressed by numerous methods that craft objectives to optimize learning progress [12, 19–25]. These approaches have demonstrated robust performance across a variety of environments.  

A broader perspective treats reinforcement learning as an inference problem [26–31]. Within this framework, variational inference for certain classes of problems has been shown to correspond to graph‑search procedures [31]. Early methods mitigate catastrophic forgetting by storing a subset of exemplars from previously seen classes and replaying them together with new data (e.g., iCaRL, GEM). Although effective, exemplar storage scales poorly because memory capacity becomes a bottleneck as the number of classes grows. To avoid explicit replay, regularization‑based techniques such as Elastic Weight Consolidation and Synaptic Intelligence constrain updates to important parameters, thereby reducing forgetting without additional storage. These methods, however, typically lag behind replay‑based approaches in accuracy. More recent work on few‑shot class‑incremental learning (FSCIL) tackles the additional challenge of learning new categories from only a few labeled examples while maintaining a limited memory budget. Despite these advances, the majority of CL methods assume that the full training set for each increment is available and fully labeled, an assumption that conflicts with the streaming, often unlabeled data encountered in real‑world robotic deployments where online learning is required.

Active learning research has focused on reducing labeling effort by allowing models to query the most informative unlabeled instances. A common strategy is uncertainty sampling, where predictive entropy, margin, or variance is used to select samples for annotation. Recent deep‑learning‑based active learning methods augment the training objective with auxiliary loss terms that encourage well‑calibrated uncertainty estimates. Nonetheless, these approaches are designed for batch learning: the model is trained on a static labeled set before querying, and the learned classifier is not updated continually. When applied in a continual setting, such methods suffer from catastrophic forgetting because they lack mechanisms to preserve knowledge of earlier tasks. Moreover, traditional active learning pipelines assume a closed‑world scenario; they can detect unknown classes only in the initial batch, after which newly encountered unknowns are forced into previously learned categories, eroding the ability to recognize novel objects in later increments.

A complementary line of research investigates open‑set recognition and out‑of‑distribution (OOD) detection, where a model trained on a known set of classes must identify samples that belong to unseen categories at test time. [ANSWER]: Fairness in machine learning has been framed along two complementary dimensions. The individual‑fairness perspective requires that similar individuals receive similar outcomes, formalized as a Lipschitz‑type condition on the predictor [2]. The group‑fairness perspective, in contrast, focuses on statistical parity across demographic groups, demanding that protected attributes not influence the distribution of predictions [1].

Approaches to achieving fairness are commonly organized into three processing stages. Preprocessing methods transform the training data so that it satisfies a chosen fairness criterion before model learning; early examples include reweighting and relabeling techniques that adjust class distributions or feature representations [3, 4]. Postprocessing methods modify the outputs of a trained model, for instance by applying calibrated thresholds or randomized decision rules to enforce demographic parity or equalized odds [5]. In‑processing methods incorporate fairness considerations directly into the learning algorithm, either by adding regularization terms, imposing constraints during optimization, or altering the model architecture; this category encompasses a wide range of algorithms that aim to reduce unfairness while preserving predictive performance [6‑9].

Within the in‑processing literature, one line of work explicitly projects an initially unfair predictor onto a set of models that satisfy fairness constraints. Such projections often measure distance between models with information‑theoretic divergences; the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence has been widely employed to define the closest fair model under various constraint formulations [10‑12]. A complementary line of research draws on optimal transport (OT) theory to quantify the cost of modifying distributions. Several recent studies have used OT barycenters—distributions that minimize the summed transport cost to each group’s empirical measure—to align group‑specific data or predictions with a common reference. These barycentric approaches have been applied to preprocessing [15], classification [11, 16] and regression [17, 18], effectively moving each demographic distribution toward a shared target. While intuitive for a small number of discrete groups, barycentric methods assume that fairness can be expressed as equality among group measures, limiting their flexibility for settings with continuous or multiple sensitive attributes and often requiring the transport cost to be a true metric.

Other works have explored unregularized OT projections onto fairness‑constrained sets, using the resulting transport cost as a diagnostic of group fairness [19]. This perspective treats the OT projection primarily as a test rather than as an integrated component of model training. Overall, the literature reflects a spectrum of strategies—from data‑level adjustments and output‑level corrections to model‑level constraints—each leveraging different notions of distance or divergence to operationalize fairness across individuals and groups.

These works showed that a single neural network can be trained to mimic the mean predictions of a large collection of models, typically by minimizing a cross‑entropy loss against the ensemble’s soft targets or by using a convex combination of the teachers’ outputs.  While effective for improving speed at test time, such approaches do not preserve the variability among ensemble members, which limits their usefulness for uncertainty quantification.  Representative examples include the original demonstrations that a student network can learn the knowledge of a big ensemble, methods that augment the standard loss with a convex combination of teacher predictions, and online student‑teacher schemes where the teacher is obtained via Markov‑chain Monte‑Carlo training.  

Subsequent research introduced techniques aimed at capturing the diversity of the teacher ensemble.  Ensemble Distribution Distillation (EnDD) was among the first to model the full predictive distribution by fitting a Dirichlet‑parameterized network to the ensemble outputs.  Building on this idea, later works also assumed a Dirichlet form for the predictive distribution, learning separate networks for the Dirichlet mean (class probabilities) and concentration (confidence).  To mitigate over‑confidence and low diversity on the training set, these methods employed unsupervised auxiliary data and temperature‑annealing schedules.  Although these approaches improve uncertainty estimates, they remain restricted to classification tasks and rely on the Dirichlet assumption, which can be overly limiting for more general predictive scenarios.  

Another line of work extended the basic distillation framework by assigning each teacher member a dedicated task head while sharing a common backbone.  In this setting the backbone learns a shared representation, and each head is trained to reproduce the predictions of a specific ensemble member using standard cross‑entropy loss.  Weight‑sharing strategies such as BatchEnsemble have also been incorporated, together with data‑perturbation schemes—including Gaussian noise, Output‑Diversified Sampling (ODS), and confidence‑aware ODS—to increase diversity among the heads on the training data. This auxiliary data is generated without requiring any external unlabeled samples, keeping the pipeline simple and scalable. Within this family, researchers have distinguished three sub‑categories: (I) methods that learn a new model while enforcing proximity to the original black‑box and fairness constraints; (II) techniques that modify the predictions of the black‑box at inference time in order to satisfy a fairness criterion; and (III) strategies that combine multiple models to obtain a fair aggregate predictor [11].

The first sub‑category comprises approaches that jointly optimize a fidelity term measuring the distance between the new model and the pretrained predictor and a fairness regularizer.
